title: Cognition Meets Le Corbusier - Cognitive Principles of Architectural Design

findings.antecedent: reference system used to encode spatial information in memory misaligned with reference system required by a particular task
findings.quote: a large cognitive cost, both in terms of speed and accuracy that occurs whenever the reference system used to encode spatial information in memory is not aligned with the reference system required by a particular task.

findings.antecedent: up-down direction of a 'You-are-here' (YAH) map coincides with the front-back direction of the observer
findings.consequent: ease of comprehending and using information depicted in YAH maps
findings.mechanism: Natural preference for directional mapping (top to front, bottom to back) is used.
findings.source: text, p. 3, citing Levine, Jankovic, & Palij (1982)
findings.quote: observers more easily comprehend and use information depicted in "You-are-here” (YAH) maps if the up-down direction of the map coincides with the front-back direction of the observer.

findings.antecedent: observer's imagined orientation during test aligned with orientation during acquisition of spatial information (from one viewpoint)
findings.consequent: ease of retrieving spatial relations between locations from memory
findings.mechanism: Alignment effects between the orientation of an observer during learning and the imagined orientation during test.
findings.quote: human observers have an easier time retrieving from memory the spatial relations between locations as seen from this viewpoint than from other, misaligned views or headings

findings.antecedent: imagined orientation during test aligned with orientation during learning (e.g., standing at 4, looking at 3, where is 2?)
findings.consequent: correctness of answers to spatial questions
findings.mechanism: Alignment effects between the orientation of an observer during learning and the imagined orientation during test.
findings.quote: Questions like “Imagine you are standing at 4, looking at 3, where is 2?” are easier to answer correctly than “Imagine you are standing at 2, looking at 4, where is 3?”.

findings.antecedent: imagined heading aligned with the first view a person has of a spatial layout during learning
findings.consequent: speed and correctness of response when recalling object locations
findings.mechanism: A person mentally represents the first view of a configuration and integrates new information from other viewpoints into this representation, leaving the original orientation intact.
findings.quote: he will be fastest and most correct in his response when imagining himself in the same heading as the first view.

findings.antecedent: imagined heading aligned with the second view a person has of a spatial layout during learning
findings.consequent: speed and correctness of response when recalling object locations
findings.mechanism: A person mentally represents the first view of a configuration and integrates new information from other viewpoints into this representation, leaving the original orientation intact.
findings.quote: Imagined headings corresponding to the second view are no better than other, not experienced headings.

findings.antecedent: imagined alignment with a square room's two main axes parallel to the walls (vs. diagonals)
findings.consequent: ease of retrieving spatial knowledge about object configuration
findings.mechanism: People are sensitive to the spatial structure of the environment.
findings.source: text, p. 5, citing Werner, Saade, & Lüer (1998)
findings.quote: she will have a much easier time retrieving the spatial knowledge about the configuration when imagining herself aligned with the room's two main axes parallel to the walls

findings.antecedent: imagined alignment with the street grid (vs. misaligned) in a large-scale city environment
findings.consequent: ease of pointing in the direction of important landmarks
findings.mechanism: People are sensitive to the spatial structure of the large-scale environment.
findings.source: text, p. 5, citing Werner & Schmidt (1999) and Montello (1991)
findings.quote: participants have a much easier time imagining themselves aligned with the street grid than misaligned with the street grid

findings.consequent: use of slant to structure spatial memories
findings.mechanism: Environmental slant provides a salient reference for spatial organization.
findings.source: text, p. 5, citing Werner (2001) and Werner, Schmidt, & Jainek (in prep.)
findings.quote: observers use environmental slant not only to communicate spatial relations verbally, but also to structure their spatial memories

findings.antecedent: imagining oneself facing uphill or downhill (aligned with steepest gradient) in a sloped environment
findings.consequent: speed and accuracy of accessing spatial knowledge about the sloped environment
findings.mechanism: Alignment with the steepest gradient of the space facilitates spatial knowledge access.
findings.quote: Accessing spatial knowledge about this sloped environment was fastest and most accurate when imagining oneself facing uphill or downhill, thus aligning oneself with the steepest gradient of the space.

findings.antecedent: floor plans with identical Inter-Connection Density (ICD) index but varying symmetry, orientation, or regularity (from left to right in Figure 3)
findings.consequent: perceived complexity of the floor plans
findings.mechanism: Figural properties beyond path options influence perceived complexity.
findings.quote: Their perceived complexity, however, rises from left to right, by making the figures less symmetric, changing the orientation, or making the figure less regular.

findings.antecedent: Göttingen town hall floor plan (with conflicting spatial reference systems, e.g., elevator area rotated 45 degrees relative to main building)
findings.consequent: difficulty to understand and navigate the building, low architectural legibility
findings.mechanism: Conflicting spatial reference systems make integration of spatial knowledge difficult.
findings.quote: Informal interviews with people working in or visiting this building revealed that it is difficult to understand and navigate. The architectural legibility is very low.

findings.antecedent: map arrangement where depicted information (street grid) was aligned with the visual vertical and horizontal
findings.consequent: ease of interpreting and using spatial information gathered from a map
findings.mechanism: Alignment with visual axes facilitates spatial information processing.
findings.quote: observers had an easier time interpreting and using spatial information gathered from a map in which the depicted information was aligned with the visual vertical and horizontal

findings.antecedent: map arrangement where depicted information (street grid) was misaligned with the visual vertical and horizontal
findings.consequent: errors in judgements about spatial relations made from memory
findings.mechanism: Misalignment with visual axes hinders spatial information processing.
findings.quote: a misalignment with these axes led to more errors in judgements about spatial relations made from memory

findings.antecedent: consistent alignment of reference axes throughout a building
findings.consequent: cognitive load for wayfinding and keeping track of position
findings.mechanism: Reduces difficulty in integrating spatial information across multiple places.
findings.quote: the consistent alignment of reference axes throughout the building, all other things being equal, will greatly reduce the cognitive load while keeping track of once position.

stimuli.description: Sample layout of objects for spatial memory task (Figure 1)
Schematic floor plans with varying ICD index (Figure 2)
Schematic floor plans with identical ICD but different perceived complexity (Figure 3)
Similar floor plans with different perceived complexity and views from within (Figure 5, top)
Geometric figures illustrating intrinsic and extrinsic reference systems (Figure 5, bottom)
Schematic floor plan of the city hall of Göttingen, Germany (Figure 6)
Schematic display of spatial situation in the town hall (Figure 7)
Maps of downtown Minneapolis (Warehouse district map, Downtown Hotels map) with different alignments

limitations: The paper primarily synthesizes and applies findings from other studies (including the authors' prior work) rather than presenting new, detailed empirical data with specific participant numbers, p-values, or effect sizes within this publication.
The concept of 'complexity' is vaguely defined and comprises different components, making its quantification challenging.
Figural complexity of a 2D floor plan may not accurately represent the navigational complexity of the 3D spatial environment.
The 'small experiment' and 'informal interviews' mentioned lack detailed methodological information (e.g., sample size, specific measures, statistical results) within this paper.
